item_name: RADIO COMMUNICATION, AIRMANSHIP, EMERGENCY PROCEDURES, GENERAL KNOWLEDGE.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - standard R/T procedures and phraseology on initial contact

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not obtain contact with the ground station following the standard procedures and phraseology. Three consecutive clearance read-backs were incorrect or omitted, and SP transmitted over an ongoing exchange between the controller and another A/C. IP had to take the radios and re-establish the approach clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology on the initial contact after each frequency change, did not use the standard format for callsign, level and intentions. Two read-backs were incomplete and were corrected only after the IP prompted on interphone, and one initial contact was made while the controller was still transmitting. R/T procedure remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed initial call after the frequency change, transmitted callsign and level in non-standard order. SP recognized the error without any prompt, re-transmitted correctly within the same exchange and used standard phraseology for the remainder of the sortie. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP established two-way communication with every station using the standard format and phraseology. Initial contact after each frequency change was made without interrupting ongoing traffic, and all clearances were read back completely and accurately on the first transmission.
texts.4: SP transmitted with complete standard phraseology throughout, including the approach clearance, the holding instruction and the missed approach. Calls were concise, correctly sequenced and consistently made in the first available gap in traffic. No transmission required repetition by the controller.
texts.marginal: SP used standard phraseology and read back all clearances correctly, but transmissions were consistently long and obliged the controller to wait for a gap. Every call was within the standard, yet the pattern trended toward occupying the frequency during the busiest phase of the approach. SP is expected to shorten the standard calls so that correct phraseology is delivered at a normal transmission rate.

texts_at.0: SP established contact with the IP transmitting the initial call in standard format on the first frequency change and prompting the format for SP to use on the second. Composing the standard call format for callsign, level and intentions without a cue has not yet been learned. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to compose and transmit the standard call independently as the format becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP established contact using the standard format, with one initial call needing a second attempt because it began while the controller was still transmitting, due to the call being made without checking the frequency for existing traffic first. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the frequency is clear before every initial call, not only after a call is stepped on.
texts_at.2: SP established contact using the standard format, with one read-back completed only after a repeat, due to a rushed initial call transmitted before the format was fully composed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compose the call fully before keying the microphone rather than starting it early.
texts_at.3: SP established two-way communication with every station using the standard format and phraseology, with one call slightly longer than the others because two items were combined, due to the callsign and level being run together under a moment of higher workload. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep every call the same length regardless of the workload at the time.

texts_above.1: SP established contact using the standard format, with one initial call needing a second attempt because it began while the controller was still transmitting. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the frequency status. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error without any prompt, re-transmitted correctly within the same exchange and used standard phraseology for the remainder of the sortie, after the callsign and level had initially been transmitted in non-standard order. Checking the format is complete before keying the microphone would remove that reordering entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good radio-format discipline.
texts_above.3: SP established two-way communication with every station using the standard format and phraseology, with initial contact made without interrupting ongoing traffic and every clearance read back completely on the first transmission. The only refinement available is to keep every call the same length regardless of the workload at the time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good radio-format discipline.
texts_above.4: SP transmitted with complete standard phraseology throughout, including the approach clearance, the holding instruction and the missed approach, with calls concise, correctly sequenced and consistently made in the first available gap in traffic. There is little left to refine; no transmission requires repetition by the controller. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent radio-format discipline.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - continuous radio watch and response timeliness

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted radio watch while re-tuning the navigation aid, did not continuously monitor radio communication. Four calls addressed to the aircraft went unanswered and the controller repeated the descent clearance twice. IP answered on behalf of the crew to prevent a loss of separation.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the approach plate, responded late to calls from the ground station. Three calls required a second transmission by the controller before SP replied, and the reply was made only after the IP prompted on interphone. Radio watch remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a cockpit task carried into the descent, missed one call from the ground station. SP recognized the missed call from the traffic on frequency, requested the transmission again without prompting and answered all subsequent calls without delay. No IP prompt was required.
texts.3: SP continuously monitored the frequency and answered every call addressed to the aircraft on the first transmission. Radio watch was maintained through the approach and through all frequency changes without a single call being missed.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted radio watch for the whole mission, answering every call immediately while continuing to fly the procedure accurately. SP also retained calls addressed to other aircraft that affected the sequence and used them to anticipate the controller's instructions.
texts.marginal: SP answered all calls within the required time, but responses during the highest workload segment of the approach were consistently at the slowest end of the acceptable range. No delay ever required a second transmission by the controller, yet the trend showed the radio watch competing with the instrument cross-check. SP is expected to hold the response time constant regardless of the workload phase.

texts_at.0: SP monitored the frequency with the IP calling attention back to the radio each time a cockpit task competed for attention on the first approach, and prompting the reply for SP to make on the second. Keeping the frequency in the scan while a cockpit task is in progress has not yet become an established habit. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to keep the frequency in the scan independently as the habit becomes established.
texts_at.1: SP monitored the frequency with three calls requiring a second transmission by the controller before the reply was made, due to attention held on the approach plate through the period the calls were transmitted. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep the frequency in the scan while the approach plate is being read, not instead of it.
texts_at.2: SP monitored the frequency with one call missed before it was recognized from the surrounding traffic, due to a cockpit task carried into the descent at the moment the call was transmitted. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to pause any cockpit task the instant a transmission on the frequency begins.
texts_at.3: SP continuously monitored the frequency and answered every call addressed to the aircraft on the first transmission, with one reply issued a beat slower than the others during the highest workload segment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same response time through the highest workload segment as through the rest of the sortie.

texts_above.1: SP monitored the frequency with three calls requiring a second transmission by the controller before the reply was made. The reply followed a verbal call from the IP naming the missed transmission. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the missed call from the traffic on frequency, requested the transmission again on its own initiative and answered all subsequent calls without delay, after one call had gone unanswered during a cockpit task. Pausing any cockpit task the instant a transmission begins would prevent that call from being missed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound radio-watch discipline.
texts_above.3: SP continuously monitored the frequency and answered every call addressed to the aircraft on the first transmission, with radio watch maintained through the approach and through all frequency changes without a single call being missed. The only refinement available is to hold the same response time through the highest workload segment as through the rest of the sortie. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed radio-watch discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted radio watch for the whole mission, answering every call immediately while continuing to fly the procedure accurately, and retained calls addressed to other aircraft that affected the sequence to anticipate the controller's instructions. There is little left to refine; the radio watch is already unbroken across the whole mission. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional radio-watch discipline.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - accurate compliance with ATC instructions

texts.0: SP, due to a clearance misinterpreted and never verified with the controller, did not precisely follow the instructions given by the ground station. SP descended to a level that had not been cleared and turned opposite to the assigned heading. IP intervened to stop the descent and to obtain a corrected clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to a clearance copied incompletely and not verified with the controller, entered the holding pattern on the wrong inbound course. The error was corrected only after two verbal directions from the IP, and the correction was applied late in the turn. Compliance remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a partially copied clearance, initially set an incorrect assigned heading. SP detected the discrepancy against the written copy, requested confirmation from the controller and complied with the correct heading before the deviation became significant. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP followed every instruction from the ground station precisely and without misinterpretation. Headings, levels and speed assignments were read back correctly and complied with promptly on each occasion.
texts.4: SP complied with every instruction exactly and immediately, including two amended clearances issued during the approach. SP verified each non-standard instruction with the controller before executing it, and no assigned parameter was ever flown incorrectly.
texts.marginal: SP complied correctly with all instructions, but on the amended clearances SP needed the full read-back to reconstruct what had been assigned before acting. Compliance stayed within standards, yet the trend showed dependence on the read-back rather than on an accurate first copy. SP is expected to copy clearances accurately at first transmission so that compliance is immediate.

texts_at.0: SP followed the instructions from the ground station with the IP verifying the clearance against the written copy on the first instruction and prompting the verification for SP to make on the second. Verifying a clearance against the written copy without a cue has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to verify and comply with clearances independently as the habit becomes established.
texts_at.1: SP followed the instructions from the ground station with one holding entry flown on the wrong inbound course before it was corrected by two verbal directions, due to a clearance copied incompletely and never verified with the controller. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to verify every clearance against the written copy before acting on it, not only the ones that seem uncertain.
texts_at.2: SP followed the instructions from the ground station with one assigned heading initially mis-set before it was corrected, due to a partially copied clearance. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to request confirmation of any clearance element that was not copied in full, at the moment it is received.
texts_at.3: SP followed every instruction from the ground station precisely and without misinterpretation, with one amended clearance requiring a second look at the written copy before it was actioned. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to action amended clearances from the first written copy with the same confidence as the original ones.

texts_above.1: SP followed the instructions from the ground station with one holding entry flown on the wrong inbound course before it was corrected by two verbal directions. The directions came as verbal calls from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the discrepancy against its own written copy, requested confirmation from the controller and complied with the correct heading before the deviation became significant, after initially setting an incorrect assigned heading. Requesting confirmation of any unclear clearance element at the moment it is received would prevent that discrepancy from developing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid clearance-verification discipline.
texts_above.3: SP followed every instruction from the ground station precisely and without misinterpretation, with headings, levels and speed assignments read back correctly and complied with promptly on each occasion. The only refinement available is to action amended clearances from the first written copy with the same confidence as the original ones. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed clearance-verification discipline.
texts_above.4: SP complied with every instruction exactly and immediately, including two amended clearances issued during the approach, verifying each non-standard instruction with the controller before executing it. There is little left to refine; no assigned parameter is ever flown incorrectly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding clearance-verification discipline.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - orientation and instrument cross-check against A/C position

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the navigation display, did not continuously monitor the control and performance instruments or crosscheck them with the A/C position. SP lost orientation in the holding pattern and allowed the aircraft to leave both the protected area and the assigned level. IP took control to re-establish the aircraft on the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of the primary flight instruments across the configuration changes, did not crosscheck aircraft performance against position. Heading and level deviations developed on three occasions and were corrected only after verbal directions from the IP, each after a noticeable delay. The cross-check remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a temporary fixation on the approach chart, allowed the cross-check to slow during the descent. SP recognized the developing deviation on the control and performance instruments, restored the scan without prompting and corrected the aircraft state before it became significant. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP continuously monitored the control and performance instruments and crosschecked them with the aircraft position throughout the mission. Orientation was maintained at all times and the required corrections were applied promptly and in the correct priority.
texts.4: SP maintained an unbroken and correctly prioritized cross-check for the whole sortie, including through configuration changes and amended clearances. Orientation with respect to the procedure was never in doubt, and corrections were anticipated rather than reactive.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation and a correct cross-check, but the scan slowed each time a new radio task arrived and corrections were applied at the late end of the acceptable range. Performance stayed within standards, yet the trend indicated that the cross-check was being displaced by secondary tasks. SP is expected to hold the cross-check rate constant while working the radios.

texts_at.0: SP monitored the control and performance instruments with the IP calling attention back to the primary flight instruments each time the navigation display competed for attention on the first descent, and prompting the cross-check for SP to run on the second. Keeping the primary flight instrument cross-check running through a navigation display task has not yet become an established habit. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running independently as the habit becomes established.
texts_at.1: SP monitored the control and performance instruments against the A/C position with three heading and level deviations developing before verbal directions corrected them, due to inadequate monitoring of the primary flight instruments across the configuration changes. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the primary flight instruments at every configuration change, not only between them.
texts_at.2: SP monitored the control and performance instruments against the A/C position with the cross-check slowing during the descent before it was restored, due to a temporary fixation on the approach chart. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the approach chart review separate from the instrument cross-check rather than combining them.
texts_at.3: SP continuously monitored the control and performance instruments and crosschecked them with the aircraft position throughout the mission, with one correction applied a beat after a radio task rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running through every radio task with the same consistency as the rest of the sortie.

texts_above.1: SP monitored the control and performance instruments against the A/C position with three heading and level deviations developing before verbal directions corrected them. The directions came as verbal calls from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the developing deviation on the control and performance instruments, restored the scan on its own initiative and corrected the aircraft state before it became significant, after the cross-check had slowed during a fixation on the approach chart. Keeping the chart review separate from the instrument cross-check would prevent that slowdown from developing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP continuously monitored the control and performance instruments and crosschecked them with the aircraft position throughout the mission, with orientation maintained at all times and required corrections applied promptly and in the correct priority. The only refinement available is to keep the cross-check running through every radio task with the same consistency as the rest of the sortie. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an unbroken and correctly prioritized cross-check for the whole sortie, including through configuration changes and amended clearances, with orientation with respect to the procedure never in doubt and corrections anticipated rather than reactive. There is little left to refine; every correction is already anticipated rather than reactive. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary cross-check discipline.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - task prioritization and saturation management

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not put the required tasks in order and became saturated. SP omitted the approach checks and the required position report while attempting to reprogram the navigation aid, and channelized attention on the equipment left the aircraft state unmonitored. IP took control and completed the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit workload inside the turn, did not handle the tasks in sequence and dropped two of them. The checks and the level-off were completed only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, each later than required. Task management remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an unexpected re-clearance, initially attempted to fly, copy and reconfigure at the same time. SP recognized the developing saturation, deferred the non-essential cockpit task and completed the remaining items in the correct order without prompting. No task was dropped and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP prioritized the cockpit tasks correctly, without omitting anything significant and without violating any rule. SP handled multiple tasks in sequence throughout the mission and never approached a channelized attention situation.
texts.4: SP maintained a correct task order throughout, including through two amended clearances and one simulated system abnormal. SP shed secondary tasks before saturation could develop and completed every required item at or before the point where it was needed.
texts.marginal: SP kept all tasks in the correct order and dropped nothing, but the margin before saturation was visibly small during the final segment of the approach. Performance remained within standards, yet the trend showed that one additional task would have displaced a required item. SP is expected to sequence cockpit work earlier so that reserve capacity is retained on the approach.

texts_at.0: SP handled the cockpit tasks with the IP deferring the non-essential task on the first busy segment and calling the task order for SP to follow on the second. Deferring a non-essential cockpit task the instant workload increases has not yet been learned. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to defer non-essential tasks and hold the task order independently as the workload becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP handled the cockpit tasks in sequence with two items dropped before repeated verbal prompting recovered them, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit workload inside the turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to spread the cockpit tasks across the approach rather than concentrating them inside a single turn.
texts_at.2: SP handled the cockpit tasks in sequence with an attempt to fly, copy and reconfigure at the same time before the sequence was corrected, due to an unexpected re-clearance arriving during a busy segment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to defer the non-essential task the instant an unexpected re-clearance arrives, not after attempting all three tasks together.
texts_at.3: SP prioritized the cockpit tasks correctly, without omitting anything significant and without violating any rule, with one task order needing a small adjustment during a busy segment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same task order through busy segments as through the rest of the sortie.

texts_above.1: SP handled the cockpit tasks in sequence with two items dropped before repeated verbal prompting recovered them. The prompting came as verbal calls from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the developing saturation, deferred the non-essential cockpit task and completed the remaining items in the correct order on its own initiative, after an unexpected re-clearance had initially prompted an attempt to fly, copy and reconfigure together. Deferring the non-essential task the instant the re-clearance arrives, rather than after attempting all three tasks, would prevent that saturation from developing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable workload management.
texts_above.3: SP prioritized the cockpit tasks correctly, without omitting anything significant and without violating any rule, handling multiple tasks in sequence throughout the mission and never approaching a channelized attention situation. The only refinement available is to hold the same task order through busy segments as through the rest of the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good workload management.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a correct task order throughout, including through two amended clearances and one simulated system abnormal, shedding secondary tasks before saturation could develop and completing every required item at or before the point where it was needed. There is little left to refine; secondary tasks are already shed before saturation develops. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior workload management.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - risk management, decision making and RTB or divert judgment

texts.0: SP, due to continuation of the plan after the weather information that invalidated it had already been received, did not identify the contingencies or the available alternatives. SP did not adjust the execution of the mission to the available flight time and remaining fuel and continued toward an airfield below minima. IP took the decision and directed the diversion.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete gathering of the available data before deciding, did not state the intended course of action clearly and could not provide the rationale for it. The alternate was selected only after two verbal directions from the IP, and the decision was taken later than the fuel state permitted. Decision making remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment that did not account for the actual holding fuel, first elected to continue for a second approach. SP re-evaluated the fuel and weather data without prompting, stated the revised decision clearly with its rationale and diverted with an adequate margin. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP accurately identified the contingencies and the available alternatives, gathered the relevant data and stated each decision clearly with its rationale. SP adjusted the execution of the mission to the available flight time and the remaining fuel, and the potential hazards were recognized and positively avoided.
texts.4: SP identified every contingency in advance, including the deteriorating destination weather, and stated the decision points before they were reached. Each decision was clearly expressed, supported by the actual data and taken early enough that all alternatives remained available.
texts.marginal: SP identified the contingencies and reached correct decisions, but each decision was taken at the last point at which it remained valid. The choices were within standards, yet the trend showed reliance on the final decision point rather than on early assessment. SP is expected to reach the same decisions earlier, while the alternatives are still unconstrained.

texts_at.0: SP reached decisions on the mission with the IP gathering the weather and fuel data on the first decision point and directing the alternate for SP to select on the second. Gathering the available data before a decision point, rather than while making the decision, has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to gather the data and reach the decision independently as the judgement becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP identified the contingencies and reached a correct decision, with the alternate selected only after two verbal directions, due to incomplete gathering of the available data before deciding. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to gather the available weather and fuel data before the decision point, not while making the decision.
texts_at.2: SP identified the contingencies and reached a correct decision, initially electing to continue before the fuel and weather data were re-evaluated, due to an initial assessment that did not account for the actual holding fuel. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the actual holding fuel against the plan before the first decision is made, not after it.
texts_at.3: SP accurately identified the contingencies and the available alternatives, gathering the relevant data and stating each decision clearly with its rationale, with one decision reached a beat later than ideal after the data was gathered. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to state the decision the moment the data is gathered rather than after a further pause.

texts_above.1: SP identified the contingencies and reached a correct decision, with the alternate selected only after two verbal directions. The directions came as verbal calls from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP re-evaluated the fuel and weather data without prompting, stated the revised decision clearly with its rationale and diverted with an adequate margin, after an initial assessment had not accounted for the actual holding fuel. Checking the actual holding fuel against the plan before the first decision, rather than after it, would remove the need for that re-evaluation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured decision-making under changing conditions.
texts_above.3: SP accurately identified the contingencies and the available alternatives, gathered the relevant data and stated each decision clearly with its rationale, adjusting the execution of the mission to the available flight time and remaining fuel. The only refinement available is to state the decision the moment the data is gathered rather than after a further pause. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise decision-making under changing conditions.
texts_above.4: SP identified every contingency in advance, including the deteriorating destination weather, and stated the decision points before they were reached, with each decision clearly expressed, supported by the actual data and taken early enough that all alternatives remained available. There is little left to refine; every decision point is already stated before it is reached. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate decision-making under changing conditions.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - flight discipline, operational checks and SOP compliance

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted check sequence that was never resumed at the correct point, did not perform the operational checks according to the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. Two required check sequences were omitted and one was performed out of order, and SP did not carry out the duties without supervision. IP had to direct and then verify the aircraft configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to check items deferred until the workload of the approach had already increased, did not carry out all the required steps of the procedures in the proper order. Three check items were completed only after being called by the IP, and the rules applicable to the approach were applied late. Flight discipline remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption caused by a frequency change, started the approach checks out of the published order. SP recognized the deviation, returned to the correct point in the sequence and completed all items without omission before commencing the descent. No IP prompt was required.
texts.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. SP demonstrated knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations and carried out all duties with minimum IP supervision.
texts.4: SP executed every check and procedure in the published sequence and at the correct point, with complete knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations. SP required no supervision at any stage and absorbed two interruptions without a single item being displaced.
texts.marginal: SP completed all checks in the correct order, but consistently started them at the latest acceptable point in the profile. Compliance remained within standards, yet the trend left no margin for an interruption before an item would be missed. SP is expected to initiate the published sequences earlier in each phase.

texts_at.0: SP carried out the required steps of the procedures with the IP running the check items before the approach workload increased on the first sortie, and calling the item for SP to complete on the second. Running check items before the approach workload increases has not yet become an established habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to run the check items independently as the habit becomes established.
texts_at.1: SP carried out the required steps of the procedures with three check items completed only after being called by the IP, due to check items deferred until the workload of the approach had already increased. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to run the check items before the approach workload increases, not once it has.
texts_at.2: SP carried out the required steps of the procedures with the approach checks started out of the published order before the sequence was corrected, due to an interruption caused by a frequency change. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to return to the correct point in the sequence the instant an interruption ends, not after the next item is also affected.
texts_at.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, with one check resumed a beat later than ideal after an interruption. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to resume every interrupted check with the same speed as the others.

texts_above.1: SP carried out the required steps of the procedures with three check items completed only after a delay, before the sequence was regained. The completion followed verbal calls from the IP naming each item still open. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the deviation, returned to the correct point in the sequence and completed all items without omission before commencing the descent, without an IP prompt, after a frequency change had interrupted the approach checks out of the published order. Returning to the correct point the instant the interruption ends, rather than after the next item is also affected, would remove that deviation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent checklist discipline.
texts_above.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, demonstrating knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations and carrying out all duties with minimum IP supervision. The only refinement available is to resume every interrupted check with the same speed as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined checklist discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed every check and procedure in the published sequence and at the correct point, with complete knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations, requiring no supervision at any stage and absorbing two interruptions without a single item being displaced. There is little left to refine; interruptions are already absorbed without displacing a single item. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless checklist discipline.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - BOLD FACE critical action recall and sequence

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the critical action procedures, did not state the BOLD FACE steps by heart or in sequence. SP reversed two steps of the simulated emergency and omitted a third, and the sequence as stated would have aggravated the condition. IP stopped the SP and performed the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete memorization of the critical action steps, stated the BOLD FACE with one step out of sequence and one omission. The sequence was corrected only after the IP prompted the missing item, and the recall was slower than the procedure requires. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitation at the transition between the memory items and the printed checklist, initially stated one BOLD FACE step out of order. SP recognized the error immediately, restated the full sequence correctly without prompting and continued from the correct point. No IP intervention was required.
